title: The Round Table
text:
The Norman poet Wace, writing his verse history of the kings of Britain around 1155, is the first writer known to mention King Arthur's Round Table.

According to Wace, Arthur's court was full of noble barons, and every one of them believed himself the best. None would accept a lower place than the others, and questions of who sat where at the king's table were a constant source of jealousy and quarrels. So Arthur had a round table made. At a round table there was no head and no foot. Every knight sat in an equal place, all were served alike, and no one could boast that he sat higher than his companions.

A few decades later the English poet Layamon expanded the story in his own Brut. In his version, a quarrel over seating at a Christmas feast turned into a bloody brawl in the king's hall. Arthur put down the fight harshly, and afterward a craftsman offered to build him a table at which a great many men could sit without any one of them being above the others.

The Round Table became the symbol of Arthur's knights, a fellowship of equals bound to the same king.
lesson: Fights over rank can poison a group of able people. Arrangements that make members visibly equal can remove the reason to quarrel.
source: Wace, Roman de Brut (c. 1155); Layamon, Brut (c. 1200)
caveat: Arthur and his table are legendary, and the origin story was told differently by later writers.
